title: Convert Binary Number in a Linked List to Integer
description: Brute force to optimized: building and parsing an intermediate string versus the direct shift-and-add technique.

content.title: Convert Binary Number in a Linked List to Integer

blocks.text: Given the head of a singly linked list, where every node's value is either 0 or 1, and the nodes represent a binary number read MOST-SIGNIFICANT-BIT FIRST, return the decimal value of this number.

blocks.caption: Each new bit shifts everything read so far left by one position, then gets added in

blocks.text: Given a linked list of 0/1 values representing a binary number (read from the most significant bit to the least significant bit), compute its decimal value.

blocks.title: Analogy: Reading Digits Aloud and Building a Number As You Go
blocks.text: Like reading the digits of a number aloud one at a time from left to right, and mentally keeping a running total: each time a new digit is heard, the running total so far is multiplied by 10 (shifting every digit heard so far one place to the left) before the new digit is added in. Binary numbers work exactly the same way, just multiplying by 2 (the base) instead of 10 at each step.

blocks.caption: This is the same digit-by-digit number-building trick used for any positional numeral system

blocks.text: Before collecting every bit into a string and parsing it as a binary number afterward, notice that the running decimal value can be built up directly, one bit at a time, using simple arithmetic.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: In any positional numeral system (decimal, binary, etc.), reading digits from most-significant to least-significant means each new digit represents one position further to the RIGHT than everything read before it.

Observation 2: Multiplying the running total by the base (2 for binary) before adding the new digit correctly shifts every previously-read digit one position to the left, making room for the new digit in the rightmost (least significant, so far) position.

Observation 3: Repeating "multiply by base, then add the new digit" for every digit in sequence, from most to least significant, correctly reconstructs the full decimal value by the time the last digit is processed.

Observation 4: This requires no intermediate string representation at all; the running numeric value itself is updated directly at each step.

Recognizing this as the standard "shift and add" technique for building up a number digit by digit, applicable to any base, avoids ever needing to construct and then parse a string.
This is the classic shift-and-add technique for parsing a positional number representation directly into its value, one digit (or bit) at a time.
Collect every bit into a string as the list is walked, then parse the completed binary string into its decimal value at the end.

items: Walk through the list, appending each node's bit value to a string.
Parse the completed binary string directly into its decimal integer value.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Bits are collected in list order, matching the required most-significant-bit-first reading order.
The completed string is only parsed once, after the full list has been walked.
Built-in base-2 parsing (e.g., int(..., 2) or parseInt(..., 2)) handles the actual conversion.

blocks.text: Every bit is collected in the correct order and the completed string is parsed correctly, so the result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to collect bits plus the cost of parsing the resulting string.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate string representation.

Limitation: building an intermediate string representation, only to immediately parse it back into a number, does unnecessary extra work when the numeric value can instead be built up directly, one bit at a time, using simple arithmetic.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force builds and then parses an intermediate string. Instead, maintain a running numeric result directly. At each node, update result to (result * 2) + node.val, which correctly shifts everything read so far left by one bit position and adds the new bit in. By the time the last node is processed, result holds the exact decimal value.
Initialize result to 0. For each node from head to the end, update result = result * 2 + node.val. Return result once the list is fully traversed.
Build the decimal value directly, one bit at a time, using the shift-and-add technique.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The running result after processing every bit is 5, matching the expected decimal value of binary 101.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, using only the single running result variable.

Every time result is multiplied by 2, every bit already incorporated into it effectively shifts one binary position to the left (since multiplying by the base is exactly how position-shifting works in any positional numeral system), freeing up the lowest bit position for the newly read bit to be added into via the + node.val. Repeating this for every bit, from most to least significant, correctly reconstructs the full binary value's decimal equivalent by the end.

blocks.text: The shift-and-add technique (multiply by the base, then add the new digit) is the fundamental way any positional numeral system's digits combine into a single value, applicable identically whether reading decimal digits, binary bits, or digits in any other base.

items: Building and parsing an intermediate string, missing the opportunity to compute the value directly with simple arithmetic.
Multiplying by the wrong base (e.g., 10 instead of 2), which would be correct for decimal digits but not for binary bits.
Processing the bits in the wrong order (least significant first), which would require reversing the list or using recursion instead of this straightforward left-to-right accumulation.

items: Name the "shift and add" technique explicitly and note that it generalizes to any base, since this framing shows understanding of the underlying number-system principle rather than just memorizing a binary-specific trick.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Convert a sequence of digits (in some base), read most-significant-first, into its numeric value" points toward the shift-and-add technique: multiply the running result by the base, then add each new digit.

items: How would this generalize to a different base (e.g., ternary, or hexadecimal)? Simply replace the multiplier of 2 with the appropriate base, and ensure each node's value is validated to be within that base's valid digit range.

How would you convert the OTHER direction, from a decimal integer back into a linked list of bits? Repeatedly take the number modulo 2 (to get the least significant bit) and integer-divide by 2, prepending each bit to a growing list, since this naturally produces bits least-significant-first.

What if the bits were given least-significant-first instead of most-significant-first? The shift-and-add technique wouldn't directly apply in the same order; instead, track a running power-of-2 multiplier and add (bit * multiplier), doubling the multiplier after each step.
The classic shift-and-add technique for positional number parsing, a broadly applicable arithmetic idea reused whenever digits (in any base) need to be combined into a single value.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (shift-and-add): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Shift-and-add, the standard technique for parsing positional number representations directly into their value
Core Idea: Multiplying the running result by the base before adding each new digit correctly shifts everything read so far and makes room for the new digit
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: This shift-and-add technique is the fundamental mechanism behind parsing ANY positional numeral system, not just binary
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: result = result * 2 + node.val, for every node
